content: ISL1, also known as Insulin gene enhancer protein ISL-1, is a protein in humans encoded by the ISL1 gene. This gene encodes a transcription factor that contains two N-terminal LIM domains and one C-terminal homeodomain. The protein plays a critical role in the embryonic development of pancreatic islets of Langerhans. In mouse embryos, a deficiency in this gene results in a failure of neural tube motor neuron differentiation. ISL1 has been shown to interact with estrogen receptor alpha. ISL1 serves as a marker for cardiac progenitor cells originating from the secondary heart field (SHF), which includes the right ventricle and the outflow tract. Its biological function has been demonstrated in Isl1 knockout mice, which exhibit severely malformed hearts. More recently, ISL1 has been identified as a marker for a cardiac progenitor cell lineage capable of differentiating into all three major cell types of the heart: cardiomyocytes, smooth muscle cells, and endothelial cells. However, the validity of ISL1 as a marker for cardiac progenitor cells has been questioned, as some studies have found no evidence that ISL1-positive cells act as cardiac progenitors. Additionally, ISL1 is not restricted to secondary heart field progenitors in the developing heart but also labels cardiac neural crest cells. This finding aligns with work from the Vilquin group in 2011, which concluded that ISL1 can represent cells from both neural crest and cardiomyocyte lineages. While multiple studies have demonstrated that ISL1-positive cells can indeed differentiate into all three major cardiac cell types, their significance in cardiovascular development remains unclear, and their clinical relevance has been seriously questioned.
